text:
Every pipeline ends by writing data somewhere. Here are a million sales, made up for this video, written twice. As a CSV file, they take thirty-nine point two megabytes. As Parquet, a columnar file format, nine point four. Ask both for revenue by category. DuckDB reads every byte of the CSV, and five megabytes of the Parquet file. Same rows, same answer: only the layout differs. Layout is what the warehousing round asks about: nine questions, from rows and columns to formats, partitions, cost and where it all lives. Seven get measured on these same rows.

Question one. What is OLTP versus OLAP, and how does storage differ? OLTP, online transaction processing, runs the application: many small reads and writes, one order at a time. So it stores each row's fields together: one order, one place. OLAP, online analytical processing, runs the reports: a few columns across millions of rows. So it stores each column together: every sale ID, then every date, and so on. Question two. Why is columnar storage faster for analytics? A query reads only the columns it names. The page's query names three of six: category, units and amount. That's why DuckDB read only five of the Parquet file's nine point four megabytes. A row format mixes those three fields in with all the rest, so the CSV was read whole. Values of one type, side by side, also compress well and run in batches.
